q: Does the França–Hashagen finite-group RB framework produce demonstrably better fidelity extraction than standard Clifford RB when applied to a hardware-native gate group whose representation is genuinely reducible (e.g., a 2-qubit iSWAP-family group, or a qutrit XX+YY gate group), where a single-exponential fit provably fails?
basis: The paper's key theoretical novelty (multi-term exponential fit whose degree equals the number of inequivalent irreps of G) is not exercised by our replication — we used single-exponential fits that would also succeed for exact 2-designs. Section 6.2 of the paper mentions this but does not include a discriminating experiment.
next_steps: Pick a specific reducible finite group G — e.g., the group generated by iSWAP + single-qubit S/X on 2 qubits, or a Cirq/Qiskit-supported hardware-native family. Enumerate its irreps via GAP (free) or a hand character-table analysis. Run RB fitted to (i) a naive single-exponential model and (ii) the paper's k-term irrep-count model. Compare fit residuals and recovered F vs analytic ground truth. A ≥2× residual-reduction from (i)→(ii) would be a discriminating positive result. Wall time estimate: ~4-8h on a single CPU node.

q: Are the paper's concentration bounds for the RB survival-probability estimator (finite-M sample-complexity regime) empirically tight, or does the true finite-sample tail probability decay faster/slower than the derived bound?
basis: We reported only point-estimator errors, not tail-probability sweeps. The paper's Theorem statements give upper bounds on Pr[|P̂_m − P_m| > ε] but do not report empirical tail-probability curves. Whether the constants are tight or loose changes practical resource-estimates for lab-scale RB campaigns.
next_steps: Fix (d, m, p) at a representative operating point, e.g., MU(8, 8), m=20, p=0.9. Sweep M ∈ {10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000} with 500 independent replicates per M-value (fully parallelizable across the m1/spark mesh via the existing sim harness). Compute empirical Pr[|Δ| > ε] for ε ∈ {10⁻⁴, 10⁻³, 10⁻²} and compare to the paper's Hoeffding-style upper bound. Also fit a data-driven exponent — if empirical scaling is faster than the bound suggests, the bound is loose and can be tightened.

q: How does the finite-group RB estimator behave under noise that explicitly breaks the group structure — e.g., non-δ-covariant noise, or noise correlated with the specific group element being applied?
basis: Both the paper and our replication assumed δ-covariant noise (a randomly rotated depolarising channel), which respects the RB decoupling. The framework's robustness under structured non-covariant noise is not established. Real-hardware crosstalk and gate-dependent noise systematically violate this assumption.
next_steps: Construct a controlled family of gate-dependent noise: T_g(ρ) = p·ρ + (1−p)·U_g ρ U_g^†, where U_g is a bounded perturbation of the ideal g. Parameterise the perturbation strength ε ∈ [0, 0.1]. Run RB on MU(4, 8) (fits inside our existing harness — modify only the noise-application step) and measure |F̂ − F_true| vs ε. Compare to the O(ε) bias predicted by first-order perturbation analysis. Free endpoint: reuse our existing monomial_rb.py + numpy stack, ~2h wall on m1.

q: Can an ML-boosted estimator (learned-basis regression, or a small transformer trained on synthetic RB trajectories) recover fidelity from shorter/fewer sequences than the paper's least-squares fit, at matched estimation error?
basis: The paper's estimator is a two-parameter exponential fit via least-squares. Modern learned estimators (e.g., simulation-based inference / neural point estimators) have been shown in adjacent noise-characterization work to achieve 2-5× sample-complexity reduction. Whether this holds for finite-group RB — where the fit function is analytically well-specified — is open.
next_steps: Generate 10⁴–10⁵ synthetic RB trajectories from our existing monomial_rb.py with p and channel drawn from a wide prior; use them to train a small MLP (or gradient-boosted regressor) that maps (P_m for m in fixed grid) → F̂. Benchmark against the exponential-fit estimator at held-out (p, σ) pairs. Metric: matched MSE at what fraction of the M budget? Free stack: scikit-learn + local PyTorch, ~4h on m1, no GPU needed.

q: Does the finite-group RB framework extend meaningfully to continuous gate sets (e.g., parameterised rotations) via a discretisation / ε-net argument, or is the discreteness of G essential to the fitting-formula derivation?
basis: The paper is explicit that G must be finite. Real hardware primitives (arbitrary-angle rotations, cross-resonance gates) are continuous. Discretising to a fine ε-net converts continuous → finite but with exponentially many elements. The framework's fitting formula complexity scales with the number of irreps; for a naive ε-discretisation of SU(d) this blows up. Whether a smarter discretisation (e.g., a T-design cover) preserves the estimator's tractability is not addressed.
next_steps: Literature review first (arxiv-sanity, semantic-scholar free tier): search for 'continuous randomized benchmarking', 'gate-set RB', 'approximate design RB' in 2019-2025. Then a minimal numerical probe: take a 1-parameter family {R_z(2πk/N) : k=0..N-1} for N ∈ {8, 16, 32, 64}, view as finite group Z_N, run our MU-style RB, and study how fitted F̂ vs N behaves as N → ∞. If F̂ converges to the underlying continuous-family fidelity, discretisation works; if it diverges or oscillates, the framework has a genuine finite-group ceiling. ~1 day of Ollie time using existing infra.
